title: High-performance orbital-torque magnetic memory on the 300-mm platform
authors: Dinggui Zeng, Yang Gao, Jinyu Duan, Lei Zhao, Yuhao An, Xing He, Jintao Ke, Yonglong Ga, Shasha Wang, Zhenghui Ji, Muyuan Chen, Hengan Zhou, Xuejie Xie, Enlong Liu, Junlu Gong, Qijun Guo, Yihui Sun, Zejie Zheng, Weiming He, Xiaolei Yang, Fantao Meng, Yaohua Wang, Hongxin Yang, Delin Zhang, Yong Jiang, Wanjun Jiang, Shikun He
abstract: Contemporary memory technologies are increasingly constrained by the fundamental trilemma of storage capacity, access latency, and power consumption. Among the emerging technologies, spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (SOT-MRAM) shows promise to circumvent these challenges, owing to its fast switching dynamics and high endurance. However, the application of SOT-MRAM is hindered by the relatively low write and read efficiencies, resulting in a large bitcell area and an insufficient sensing margin. Meanwhile, the involvement of an ultrathin spin-source channel, typically within a few nanometers, imposes technological challenges for mass production. Here, we resolve these issues on a 300-mm wafer platform by exploiting the emerging orbital degree of freedom and the resultant orbital torque (OT) from the relatively thick Ti/W bilayer. In particular, OT memory nanodevices exhibit a giant tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) of 182%, nanosecond-scale response, 1012 endurance, together with an enhanced switching efficiency (E_b/I_c), which consequently enables an ultra-low write energy of less than 0.1 pJ/bit. Our findings demonstrate that orbital angular momentum can be implemented for building energy-efficient MRAM devices, offering a practical pathway towards low-latency memory that is demanded for high-performance computing and AI applications.
summary: This work presents a high-performance magnetic memory utilizing orbital-torque (OT) effects in a Ti/W bilayer structure on a large-scale 300-mm wafer. By leveraging the orbital angular momentum, the authors achieved ultra-low write energy and high TMR, offering a practical pathway for next-generation, energy-efficient memory for AI and high-performance computing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental limitations of existing memory technologies, specifically the trade-off between storage capacity, access latency, and power consumption in SOT-MRAM.
main_result: They demonstrate that utilizing orbital torque (OT) in a Ti/W bilayer structure enables MRAM devices with giant TMR (up to 182%), ultra-low write energy (< 0.1 pJ/bit), and high endurance.
method: The research combines extensive experimental characterization (TMR measurement, ST-FMR, endurance testing) with first-principles theoretical calculations (calculating orbital and spin Hall conductivities).
model_or_system: The physical system is an orbital-torque magnetic random-access memory (OT-MRAM) device built on a scalable 300-mm wafer platform, utilizing a pMTJ stack with a Ti/W bilayer as the orbital-current channel.
key_observables: TMR ratio (up to 182%), write energy (< 0.1 pJ/bit), endurance ($10^{12}$ cycles), and orbital-to-spin conversion efficiency ($\xi_{OT}$).
important_parameters: 300-mm wafer platform, Ti/W bilayer thickness optimization (e.g., $t_W = 1.5$ nm), and low critical switching current densities ($J_c$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that exploiting the orbital degree of freedom via the Ti/W interface can overcome the efficiency and scaling issues inherent in traditional SOT-MRAM.
figures_summary: Figures show wafer-scale TMR mapping, R-V loops demonstrating switching, and plots detailing the dependence of $\xi_{OT}$ and write energy on material parameters and pulse width.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of identifying the memory bottleneck, proposing the orbital-torque mechanism using Ti/W, presenting comprehensive experimental validation across read/write/endurance metrics, and supporting these findings with first-principles calculations of transport properties.
why_interesting: While focused on spintronics/materials science, the underlying physics involves spin-orbit coupling and emergent magnetic torques, which are crucial areas of study in condensed matter theory related to topological materials and quantum transport.
